title: Number System
shortDescription: Divisibility, HCF/LCM, remainders and unit digits — the classification and shortcut toolkit almost every other Quant topic quietly leans on.
genZNote: Numbers really said 'I have categories' and then made us memorise all of them. Here's the cheat-code version — five tools, reused forever.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Number System questions are rarely about the classification chart itself — they test whether you can quickly tell what a number IS (prime? divisible by 8? what remainder does it leave?) without doing full division every time. The exam-useful skill is five tools: divisibility rules, HCF/LCM by prime factorisation, the HCF×LCM shortcut, modular remainder reduction, and unit-digit/cyclicity patterns.

sections.heading: Number Types — the 30-Second Version
bullets: Natural numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) ⊂ Whole numbers (0, 1, 2, ...) ⊂ Integers (..., −1, 0, 1, ...) ⊂ Rational numbers (expressible as p/q) ⊂ Real numbers.
Irrational numbers (√2, π — non-terminating, non-repeating decimals) sit outside rationals but still inside reals.
Prime: exactly two factors (1 and itself). 2 is the only even prime. 1 is neither prime nor composite.

rows: Last two digits form a number divisible by 4
Difference of (sum of digits at odd places) and (sum of digits at even places) is 0 or a multiple of 11

sections.heading: HCF & LCM — Method and the Fast Shortcut

steps.name: Prime factorisation method
steps.explanation: Break every number into prime factors. LCM = product of the HIGHEST power of every prime appearing in ANY of the numbers. HCF = product of the LOWEST power of every prime common to ALL numbers.
steps.purpose: The reliable, always-works method — use when numbers are small enough to factorise quickly.

steps.name: The a × b shortcut
steps.explanation: For any two numbers a and b: HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b. If you already have one of HCF/LCM and the product a×b, the other falls out by division — no need to factorise at all.
steps.purpose: Fastest exam path when the question gives you one of the two plus the numbers themselves.

sections.heading: Remainders — Reduce Before You Multiply
sections.body: For 'find the remainder when [large product or power] is divided by n', reduce EACH factor modulo n first, then multiply or exponentiate, then reduce again. This keeps every intermediate number small instead of building one enormous product you then have to divide.
bullets: Example: remainder of (17 × 23) ÷ 5. 17 mod 5 = 2, 23 mod 5 = 3. 2 × 3 = 6, 6 mod 5 = 1. Remainder = 1 — no need to compute 17×23 = 391 at all.

sections.heading: Unit Digit & Cyclicity of Powers
sections.body: The unit digit of aⁿ repeats in a cycle. Digits 0, 1, 5, 6 never change (cycle length 1). Digits 4, 9 cycle with length 2. Digits 2, 3, 7, 8 cycle with length 4. To find the unit digit of aⁿ: find the cycle length for a's unit digit, then compute n mod (cycle length) — using that remainder (or the cycle length itself if the remainder is 0) tells you which position in the cycle to read off.

steps.name: Worked example — standard method
steps.explanation: Find the unit digit of 7^45. Powers of 7 cycle every 4: 7¹=7, 7²=49, 7³=343, 7⁴=2401 → unit digits 7,9,3,1, repeating.

steps.name: Worked example — fast method
steps.explanation: 45 mod 4 = 1, so 7^45 has the same unit digit as 7¹.
steps.purpose: Unit digit = 7 — found without computing anything close to 7^45.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Taking the LOWEST prime power for LCM and the HIGHEST for HCF — it's the reverse: LCM wants highest, HCF wants lowest.
Applying the HCF×LCM = a×b shortcut to THREE or more numbers — it's only valid for exactly two numbers.
Forgetting that when n mod (cycle length) = 0, you use the LAST digit of the cycle, not a 'zeroth' position — e.g. 7^44: 44 mod 4 = 0, so use the 4th cycle digit (1), not treat it as undefined.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: For divisibility questions, apply the specific rule directly rather than doing long division — it's almost always faster.
For 'find the remainder' questions with large numbers, reduce modulo the divisor at every step rather than computing the full product/power first.
For unit-digit questions, find the cycle length (1, 2, or 4) for the base's last digit before doing anything else with the exponent.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Number System covers classifying numbers and applying divisibility, HCF/LCM, remainder, and unit-digit shortcuts instead of raw calculation.
keyFacts: LCM: highest prime power present anywhere. HCF: lowest prime power common to all.
HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b — valid for exactly two numbers.
Reduce factors modulo n before multiplying/exponentiating for remainder questions.
commonConfusion: 1 is neither prime nor composite — a very common exam trap in 'how many primes between 1 and 20' style questions.
2 is the only even prime; every other even number is composite.

highYieldFacts: HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b for any two numbers — reused constantly across Number System and Ratio problems.
Unit-digit cyclicity has exactly three cycle lengths to remember: 1, 2, and 4.
commonTraps: Swapping which of LCM/HCF takes the highest vs lowest prime power.
Using the a×b = HCF×LCM shortcut on more than two numbers, where it does not hold.
mustRemember: Divisibility by 11: alternating digit-sum difference must be 0 or a multiple of 11.
1 is neither prime nor composite; 2 is the only even prime.

confusedTerms.distinction: HCF is the largest number dividing all given numbers (lowest common prime powers); LCM is the smallest number divisible by all given numbers (highest prime powers present anywhere).

possibleQuestions: Find the HCF and LCM of two numbers given their product and one of the two.
Find the remainder when a large power is divided by a small number.
Find the unit digit of a large power.
